name: Blood count + hemoglobin test
full: CBC with HPLC or electrophoresis
purpose: Finds carriers of common hemoglobin disorders: β-thalassemia trait, sickle cell trait, HbE.
who: Couples before marriage or pregnancy, early pregnancy, relatives of someone affected.
detects: β-thalassemia trait, HbS, HbE, HbD and other common variants.
limits: Can miss α-thalassemia carriers and silent β-carriers; iron deficiency can mask results. DNA testing may be needed.
india: Among the most common inherited conditions in India. Low-cost and widely available.
ask: Can we both get a CBC and HPLC done, and how should borderline results be followed up?

name: Targeted carrier screening
full: DNA test for a chosen set of recessive conditions
purpose: Checks if you carry a change for selected conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy.
who: People planning a family, especially with family history or related partners.
detects: Carrier status for the listed conditions only.
limits: A negative result lowers but does not remove the chance of being a carrier.
gc: If a carrier result is found.
india: Choose conditions by family history and region, never by community labels.
ask: Which conditions would you include in carrier screening for our family, and why?

name: Expanded carrier screening
full: Panel of tens to hundreds of recessive conditions
purpose: Screens many recessive conditions at once.
who: Optional before pregnancy; more often discussed when partners are related.
detects: Carrier status for panel conditions (panels differ by lab).
limits: Can find uncertain variants; most findings matter only if both partners carry the same gene.
india: Coverage of variants common in Indian families varies by lab.
ask: Would an expanded panel add anything useful for us compared with targeted screening?

name: Partner testing
full: Testing the partner of a known carrier for the same condition
purpose: Finds out whether both partners carry a change for the same recessive condition.
who: Partner of someone known to be a carrier.
detects: Carrier status for the same condition (for hemoglobin: CBC + HPLC, sometimes DNA).
limits: For HBB, different variants (β-thal, HbS, HbE) can combine, so the partner's report must cover all of them.
india: The single most useful step after one partner is found to be a thalassemia or sickle carrier.
ask: My partner is a carrier. Which test should I have so that all relevant variants are covered?

name: Known family variant test
full: Testing for the exact change found in a relative
purpose: Tells relatives whether they carry the change already identified in the family.
who: Relatives of someone with a confirmed genetic diagnosis.
detects: That one specific variant.
limits: Answers only that question. Needs the relative's lab report.
india: Usually the most informative and cheapest option when a family variant is known.
ask: Here is my relative's report. Can I be tested for this exact variant?

name: Karyotype
full: Chromosome analysis
purpose: Finds large chromosome changes, including balanced rearrangements.
who: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss; suspected chromosome conditions.
detects: Extra or missing chromosomes, translocations, large deletions.
limits: Low resolution; misses small and single-gene changes.
india: Widely available.
ask: Should both of us have a karyotype because of the repeated losses?

name: Ultrasound + maternal blood screening
full: Routine antenatal scans and serum screening
purpose: Estimates the chance of selected chromosomal conditions and checks the baby's structure.
who: All pregnant women.
detects: Higher or lower chance of trisomy 21 and others; visible anomalies.
limits: Gives a chance, not a diagnosis. Many genetic conditions are not visible on scan.
india: Availability varies between public and private settings.
ask: Which screening tests are due now, and what happens if a result shows a high chance?

name: NIPT
full: Cell-free DNA screening from the mother's blood
purpose: More sensitive screening for trisomies 21, 18 and 13.
who: Pregnant women, usually from about ten weeks.
detects: High or low chance of the conditions tested.
limits: Still screening. A high-chance result must be confirmed by CVS or amniocentesis. Does not cover most single-gene conditions.
india: Mostly private labs, paid separately.
ask: Is NIPT useful in my situation, and what would a high-chance result mean next?

name: CVS or amniocentesis
full: Diagnostic prenatal sampling with genetic testing
purpose: Confirms or rules out a specific condition in the baby.
who: High-chance screening, scan anomaly, or a known family condition.
detects: Depends on the test run on the sample: chromosomes, a family variant, or more.
limits: Small procedure risk. CVS is usually done around 10–13 weeks and amniocentesis from about 15 weeks.
india: Done by fetal medicine specialists; timing matters, so ask early.
ask: Is diagnostic testing advised, which test fits my weeks, and which lab tests would be run on the sample?

name: Newborn screening
full: Heel-prick dried blood spot
purpose: Finds treatable conditions before symptoms start.
who: All newborns, usually in the first few days.
detects: Conditions on the local panel, which may include congenital hypothyroidism, CAH, G6PD deficiency, galactosemia, PKU.
limits: Panels differ across states and hospitals. A positive screen needs confirmation.
india: Ask which conditions your hospital covers.
ask: Which conditions does this hospital's newborn screening include, and when will we get results?

name: Chromosomal microarray
full: Scan for small missing or extra chromosome pieces (CNVs)
purpose: Finds copy-number changes linked to developmental delay and birth differences.
who: Children with unexplained delay, ID or multiple anomalies.
detects: Deletions and duplications.
limits: Misses single-letter changes and balanced rearrangements.
india: Widely available; exome is increasingly used alongside it.
ask: Would microarray or exome be the better first test for my child?

name: Targeted gene panel
full: Sequencing genes linked to one clinical problem
purpose: Looks for a cause among known genes for epilepsy, hearing, retina, muscle, heart, immunity.
who: People with a clear clinical picture matching the panel.
detects: Changes in the listed genes.
limits: Genes not on the panel are not examined.
india: Often cheaper and faster than exome when the picture is clear.
ask: Is a targeted panel enough, or would exome give a better chance of an answer?

name: Whole-exome sequencing
full: Most protein-coding regions (~1–2% of the genome)
purpose: Searches for the cause of a suspected rare genetic condition across most genes.
who: People with features of a genetic condition, often children. Trio WES includes both parents.
detects: Pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants; some labs also report CNVs and mitochondrial variants.
limits: A negative result does not rule out a genetic condition. Can find VUS. Reanalysis later may help.
india: Indian variants are under-represented in public databases.
ask: Should we do trio exome, and will the lab reanalyse the data later if nothing is found?

name: Whole-genome sequencing
full: Almost the entire genome
purpose: Broadest single test for suspected rare conditions.
who: Selected cases, often critically ill infants or after a negative exome.
detects: Sequence changes, CNVs, many structural variants, mtDNA if analysed.
limits: More data is not always more answers; more VUS and higher cost.
india: Fewer labs; usually costs more than exome.
ask: After a negative exome, is genome sequencing or reanalysis the better next step?

name: Hereditary cancer panel
full: BRCA1/2, Lynch syndrome genes and others
purpose: Finds inherited changes that raise risk of certain cancers.
who: People with cancer meeting criteria, or relatives with strong family history or a known variant.
detects: Germline pathogenic variants in panel genes.
limits: Most cancers are not caused by one inherited change. Different from routine cancer screening.
india: Criteria-based testing is more informative than testing everyone.
ask: Does my personal or family history meet criteria for hereditary cancer testing? Should an affected relative be tested first?

name: Inherited heart condition testing
full: FH, cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia genes
purpose: Confirms an inherited cause and lets relatives be tested.
who: Very high LDL, early heart attacks or young sudden death in the family, cardiomyopathy.
detects: Variants in LDLR, APOB, PCSK9 or heart muscle and rhythm genes.
limits: Clinical tests come first (lipid profile, ECG, echo).
india: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is thought to be under-diagnosed.
ask: Could this be familial hypercholesterolaemia or an inherited heart condition, and should my relatives be checked?

name: Pharmacogenomic test
full: Genes that affect how you handle certain medicines
purpose: Helps a doctor choose a medicine or dose for selected drugs.
who: People starting medicines with established gene–drug guidance.
detects: CYP2C19, CYP2C9/VKORC1, HLA-B, DPYD, TPMT/NUDT15 and others.
limits: Only some drugs have strong guidance. Never change a medicine on your own.
india: HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine is relevant in parts of South and Southeast Asia.
ask: Is there a gene test recommended before I start this medicine?

name: Polygenic risk score
full: Many common variants combined for one disease
purpose: Estimates relative inherited susceptibility to diseases like type 2 diabetes.
who: Education and research; not a routine clinical test in India yet.
detects: Where your score sits versus a reference population.
limits: Not a diagnosis. Mostly built on European data and may be less accurate for South Asians.
india: Must be compared against a South Asian reference.

name: Celiac disease blood test
full: tTG-IgA antibody with total IgA (HLA-DQ2/DQ8 gene test only in special cases)
purpose: Checks whether wheat, barley or rye (gluten) is damaging the gut.
who: People with loose motions, weight loss, poor growth or anaemia that doesn't improve with iron, and close relatives of someone with celiac disease.
detects: Antibodies that are raised in celiac disease. A gut biopsy usually confirms the diagnosis.
limits: Only works while you are still eating wheat. The HLA gene test cannot diagnose celiac disease: many healthy people carry these genes. A negative HLA test makes celiac disease very unlikely.
india: More common in North India, where wheat is a staple food.
ask: Should I be tested for celiac disease before I change my diet?

name: Milk (lactose) intolerance check
full: Dairy-free trial or hydrogen breath test; LCT gene test rarely needed
purpose: Finds out whether milk sugar (lactose) causes your symptoms.
who: People who get bloating, gas or loose motions after milk.
detects: Whether symptoms settle without milk, or whether lactose is poorly digested on a breath test.
limits: The common LCT gene marker was found in European populations and does not capture all the variants in South Asians, so a gene result can be misleading. Many people who digest lactose poorly can still have curd and small amounts of milk.
india: Many adults in India digest lactose less well than children do. This is normal and is not a disease.
ask: Could my symptoms be lactose intolerance, or something else?

name: G6PD test
full: G6PD enzyme activity blood test
purpose: Checks for G6PD deficiency, where red blood cells break down after certain medicines, infections or fava beans.
who: People with dark urine, yellow eyes or sudden tiredness after fava beans or some medicines; newborns with jaundice; relatives of someone with G6PD deficiency.
detects: Low G6PD enzyme activity.
limits: Can read falsely normal soon after a breakdown episode. Women can have a partial deficiency that is easy to miss, and a gene test may help them.
india: G6PD deficiency is found across India and is checked in some newborn screening programmes.
ask: Are there medicines or foods I should avoid?

name: Nutrigenomics ("DNA diet") test
full: Gene panels sold for diet, weight or vitamin advice (e.g. MTHFR, FTO, APOE)
purpose: Claims to tailor your diet to your genes.
who: Not recommended for routine use.
detects: Common gene variants, each with a very small effect on weight, cholesterol or vitamin levels.
limits: In a large trial, DNA-based diet advice worked no better than advice based on what people actually eat. MTHFR testing is not recommended. Blood tests (sugar, lipids, B12, vitamin D) are more useful.
india: Widely sold in India, often with a lot of marketing.
ask: Would a blood test tell us more than a DNA diet test?

name: Genetic counselling
full: Consultation with a genetic counsellor or clinical geneticist
purpose: Helps you decide whether and how to test, and what results mean.
who: Known family variant, affected child, related partners, abnormal screening, complex history.
detects: Not a test.
limits: Usually paid in private settings; some government genetics departments offer it.
india: Available in medical genetics departments of larger hospitals.
ask: Can you refer me to a genetic counsellor or clinical geneticist?
